---
title: "Random effects and partial pooling"
execute: {warning: false, message: false}
---

We have separated [population and group terms](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd): the population coefficients describe the shared relation, while listener and word deviations describe departures from it. The remaining question is how much evidence the data provide about each deviation. Estimating every listener in isolation can chase noise, while assigning every listener the same value erases genuine variation. [**Partial pooling**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-hierarchical.html) is the compromise produced when the listener estimates are fit together under a shared population distribution.

The group distribution uses [variance and standard deviation](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) to describe deviations we do not observe directly, while a [residual](residuals.qmd) is the remaining observed minus fitted trial response. MALD has [crossed units](structured-data.qmd): listeners respond to multiple words, and words receive responses from multiple listeners. Each estimated deviation therefore summarizes behavior under this lexical decision task rather than an intrinsic person or word trait.

We first derive complete, no, and partial pooling for one scalar deviation. We then compute the corresponding MALD estimates and state the exchangeability assumption that makes the shared distribution meaningful.

## Model deviations from a shared center

Begin with a crossed intercept-only model for the correct MALD latencies:

$$
Y_{pwi}=\beta_0+b_p+c_w+\varepsilon_{pwi},
$$

where

$$
b_p\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_p^2),\qquad
c_w\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_w^2),\qquad
\varepsilon_{pwi}\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2).
$$

The zero centers define $\beta_0$ as the population center. They do not assert that participants or words are identical. The parameters $\tau_p$ and $\tau_w$ describe the extent of persistent baseline differences.

## Comparing pooling strategies

Complete pooling ignores participant identity and assigns every participant the population baseline $\beta_0$. No pooling estimates an unrelated mean for every participant. Partial pooling gives each participant a distinct deviation while estimating those deviations under one population distribution.

For a normal random intercept model with one grouping unit and known variance components, the participant deviation has the form

$$
\widehat b_p
=w_p(\overline y_p-\beta_0),
$$

with

$$
w_p
=\frac{n_p\tau_p^2}{\sigma^2+n_p\tau_p^2}.
$$

The weight $w_p$ lies between zero and one. More observations or greater variation across participants move it toward one; more residual variation within participants moves it toward zero. The likelihood supplies evidence about this participant, and the shared normal distribution supplies information about the population of participant deviations. Conditioning on both places each conditional mode between the unpooled participant difference and the population center; no separate correction is applied after fitting.

To derive the expression, condition on all other model terms and write the
participant contribution to the negative log likelihood, up to constants, as
the expression below. Recall that a
[likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd) treats the observed
responses as fixed while the participant deviation and population parameters
vary.

$$
Q(b_p)=\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n_p}(y_{pi}-\beta_0-b_p)^2
+\frac{b_p^2}{2\tau_p^2}.
$$

Differentiating and setting the result to zero gives

$$
-\frac{n_p(\bar y_p-\beta_0-b_p)}{\sigma^2}+\frac{b_p}{\tau_p^2}=0,
$$

which solves to the weight above. This algebra resembles normal–normal posterior updating, but `lmer` treats the fitted population and variance parameters frequentistically and reports a conditional mode.

The variances in that expression must themselves be estimated. Recall that the
[Gaussian mixed model likelihood](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd#gaussian-mixed-model-likelihood)
averages over the participant and word deviations, then uses REML to estimate
the covariance parameters after accounting for the population coefficient
directions. The scalar weight is exact for the one-group model with known
variances. In the crossed MALD model, all participant and word modes solve one
joint penalized problem, to which we return when we examine
[conditional modes](random-effect-estimates.qmd#defining-the-conditional-mode).

## Computing the three MALD summaries

```{r}
#| label: mald-partial-pooling
library(lme4)
library(ggplot2)

mald <- read.csv("data/mald/mald-connected-trials.csv")
mald <- subset(mald, correct == 1L)

fit <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ 1 +
    (1 | participant_id) +
    (1 | item),
  data = mald,
  REML = TRUE,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

raw_means <- aggregate(
  log_rt ~ participant_id,
  data = mald,
  FUN = mean
)
names(raw_means)[names(raw_means) == "log_rt"] <- "raw_mean"

participant_modes <- ranef(fit)$participant_id
partial_means <- data.frame(
  participant_id = rownames(participant_modes),
  partially_pooled_mean =
    fixef(fit)[["(Intercept)"]] + participant_modes[["(Intercept)"]],
  row.names = NULL
)

pooling <- merge(raw_means, partial_means, by = "participant_id")
pooling$complete_pooling_mean <- fixef(fit)[["(Intercept)"]]
pooling$movement_toward_center <- with(
  pooling,
  abs(raw_mean - complete_pooling_mean) -
    abs(partially_pooled_mean - complete_pooling_mean)
)

summary(pooling$movement_toward_center)

pooling[c(
  which.max(pooling$movement_toward_center),
  which.min(pooling$movement_toward_center)
), ]
```

The two displayed MALD participants show that the movement is estimated from the observed trial histories rather than imposed as one common adjustment. The first moves the greatest absolute distance toward the fitted center, while the second moves the least.

```{r}
#| label: plot-mald-pooling
ggplot(
  pooling,
  aes(x = raw_mean, y = partially_pooled_mean)
) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = fixef(fit)[["(Intercept)"]],
    color = "#1F5A85",
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 1.3) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    x = "Raw participant mean log response time",
    y = "Partially pooled participant mean"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

The diagonal marks equality between raw and partially pooled means. Points move toward the horizontal population center, with the amount of movement determined by the fitted variances and the information available for each listener.

## Keeping two kinds of variation separate

The participant standard deviation $\tau_p$ describes stable variation across listeners. The residual standard deviation $\sigma$ describes trial variation around participant and word baselines. These sources answer different questions: $\tau_p$ concerns persistent listener differences, while $\sigma$ concerns fluctuations among trials after the modeled baselines are supplied.

## Understanding exchangeability

Recall that [exchangeability](../statistical-inference/posterior-distributions.qmd#a-bernoulli-superpopulation-model)
means that relabeling observational units leaves their joint distribution
unchanged. Here the units are participants, and the shared normal distribution
treats their labels as exchangeable after conditioning on included predictors.
Before observing the responses, swapping two arbitrary participant labels does
not change the model. If listeners differ systematically by a measured
property, that property should enter the population relation; the random effects
then describe remaining variation.

For instance, exchanging any two participant identifiers everywhere leaves the model unchanged. Changing a measured bilingual-status value would not: if bilingual status predicts response time, it belongs in the population relation rather than being hidden inside exchangeable residual heterogeneity.

```{r}
#| label: two-participant-shrinkage-weights
#| echo: true
counts <- sort(table(mald$participant_id))
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit))
tau2 <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "participant_id" & is.na(vc$var2)]
sigma2 <- sigma(fit)^2
n_examples <- c(smallest = unname(counts[1]), largest = unname(counts[length(counts)]))
data.frame(trials = n_examples,
           shrinkage_weight = n_examples * tau2 / (sigma2 + n_examples * tau2))
```

The displayed weights insert the fitted participant and residual variances into
the one-group formula. They are reference calculations rather than the exact
weights of the crossed participant-by-word fit, whose joint solution also
depends on which words each listener heard.

An estimated deviation near zero can indicate either that a listener lies near the fitted center or that the listener's trials provide weak information and receive strong shrinkage. The estimate, its conditional uncertainty, and the number of trials must be interpreted together.

## Recap and check

1. Does partial pooling move every raw mean by the same amount? No. The weight depends on $n_p$ and the fitted within- and between-participant variances.
2. Does exchangeability assert that listeners are identical? No. It says their labels carry no further model information after conditioning on included predictors.

We next derive the dependence induced when repeated rows contain the same [random intercept](random-intercepts.qmd).
